title: One-dimensional Dirac modes in the core of a pentagonal topological crystalline insulator nanowire
authors: Saeed Samadi, Rafał Rechciński, Marta A. Chabowska, Ryszard Buczko
abstract: We investigate the electronic band topology of recently fabricated pentagonal IV-VI semiconductor nanowires, which contain five radial $\{111\}$ twin planes meeting at the nanowire axis. Tight-binding calculations show that, when the bulk band structure is inverted and the twin planes in the nanowire are cationic, the spectrum contains two spatially separated helical Dirac crossings near $\overlineΓ$: one localized at the core and the other at the outer surface. When the twin planes are anionic, the corresponding spectra remain gapped. The crossings originate from the hybridization of five helical channels associated with the twin-plane edges, whose odd number leaves one Kramers pair near the nanowire axis and the other at the outer boundary. Realistic multiorbital calculations for $\mathrm{Pb}_{0.4}\mathrm{Sn}_{0.6}\mathrm{Te}$ predict well-developed core and surface modes at nanowire thicknesses of approximately 50~nm and above. These results establish pentagonal SnTe-class nanowires as an experimentally accessible realization of spatially separated helical channels bound to the axial defect and the outer boundary.
summary: This work theoretically examines pentagonal topological crystalline insulator nanowires, predicting the existence of two spatially separated helical Dirac crossings—one localized in the core and one on the outer surface. These crossings appear only when the twin planes are cationic and the bulk band structure is inverted. The findings establish these specific nanowire geometries as a promising platform for realizing distinct boundary-bound topological states.
main_problem: The study investigates the electronic band topology of pentagonal topological crystalline insulator (TCI) nanowires, aiming to identify spatially separated helical Dirac crossings.
main_result: When the twin planes are cationic and bulk band inversion occurs, two distinct helical Dirac crossings—one at the core and one on the outer surface—are predicted. This establishes these structures as an accessible platform for realizing such separated topological channels.
method: The research employs tight-binding (TB) calculations, supplemented by low-energy k·p theory, to model the electronic band structure of the nanowires.
model_or_system: The system is a pentagonal IV–VI semiconductor nanowire (e.g., SnTe-class), characterized by five radial {111} twin planes meeting at the axis. The analysis compares results based on whether these twin planes are cationic or anionic.
key_observables: Electronic band structure, presence/absence of Dirac crossings, and wave function localization (core vs. surface).
important_parameters: Cationic vs. anionic composition of the twin planes; nanowire thickness ($\ge 50$ nm for predictions); bulk band inversion.
main_assumptions: The calculations neglect axial strain from transverse deformation and use idealized core structures, which may not reflect true relaxation states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate band structures showing the emergence of core/surface Dirac crossings (Fig. 3) and demonstrate that these crossings can arise even when considering only a single cationic twin plane shell (Fig. 4).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical framework using TB models, then analyzing the spectral consequences based on the sublattice composition of the twin planes, and finally discussing structural stability via binding energy calculations.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state topology, the concept of spatially separated boundary modes (core vs. surface) is analogous to engineered quantum systems where confinement dictates distinct physical behaviors at different spatial locations.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Geometry of the pentagonal IV–VI NW. (a) Rocksalt crys- tal structure. (b) Fivefold-twinned NW grown along the [011] di- rection, composed of five wedge-shaped rocksalt domains separated by radial {111} TPs and terminated by five {100} outer facets. The TPs are either all cationic or all anionic and meet along the NW axis. (c) Cross section formed from undistorted domain wedges, for which the crystallographic angle between neighboring {111} planes is 70.53◦, leaving an angular deficit of 1.47◦per domain. (d) Reg- ular pentagonal cross section obtained by deforming each wedge to an opening angle of 72◦. (e) Side view of one trigonal-prismatic domain.

FIG. 2. Reciprocal-space geometry of the pentagonal NW. (a) Perspective view of one trigonal-prismatic domain along the NW growth direction. (b) Three-dimensional fcc Brillouin zone and the one-dimensional Brillouin zone associated with translation along [011]. For each domain, the four bulk L points project pairwise onto Γ at the center and Z at the boundary of the one-dimensional Brillouin zone. The five rotated domains share the same axial Bril- louin zone.

FIG. 3. Band structures and wave-function localization in pentagonal SnTe NWs. Panels (a) and (b) show the spectra of 14 nm-thick (20-ring) NWs with cationic and anionic TPs, respectively; the inset schematics illustrate the corresponding three-ring structures for clarity. Red and blue color intensi- ties indicate wave-function weight near the core and the outer surface. In panel (b), a local onsite-energy shift of 40 meV is applied to orbitals within 1 nm of the NW axis to move a topologically trivial core-localized subband away from the small surface gap; the unshifted spectrum is not shown. Pan- els (c) and (d) show the probability densities of the core- and surface-localized states...

FIG. 4. Band structures of cylindrical SnTe shells containing a single (a) cationic and (b) anionic TP. The calculated shells are 18 atomic layers thick and contain 40 atoms around the outer circumference. Red and blue color intensities indicate wave-function weight near the inner and outer surfaces, re- spectively. The inset schematics show four-layer shells with 12 atoms around the outer circumference; the twisted peri- odic boundary is represented by bending each shell into its closed form to make the common My mirror plane explicit. Panel (c) illustrates the construction of the twisted boundary condition using a four-layer shell with 14 atoms around the outer circumference.

FIG. 5. Band structures of pentagonal SnTe NWs after apply- ing time-reversal-preserving perturbations to the outermost atomic layers. Panels (a) and (b) correspond to NWs with cationic and anionic TPs, respectively. The inset schematics indicate the perturbed surface regions, with P denoting per- turbations that break the vertical My mirror symmetries of the NW in the surface region.
